title: Emaki 絵巻
section: From the IDE to the ADE
text:
From the IDE to the ADE



               Activity Bar       File Browser      Outline     Timeline            Code             Terminal         Agent Chat            




IDE integrated development environment

An IDE is the traditional way to work on code: built for writing it by hand, with many panels and a steep learning curve. With agents, the chat does most of the work, yet the editor still takes the middle of the screen and the chat gets a narrow pane at the edge.







       Emaki                             New Chat     Projects                    Chats       Agent Chat                                Files             Outline            Shell Terminal            Agent Terminal   




ADE agentic development environment

Emaki turns this around. The agent chat takes the main space, and the sidebar groups your sessions under their projects. The supporting panels (files, outline and the two terminals) stay hidden until you need them.

title: Emaki 絵巻
text:
Main system
Sessions are listed and managed under their projects. The agent chat takes the main space, rendered in high quality.

title: Emaki 絵巻
text:
Panels
Emaki provides 4 panels, hidden by default, since they are essential but used less often than the chat.

title: Settings
text:
Appearance and Fonts
Appearance follows the system, or stays light or dark. The accent is one of seven colors: periwinkle, orchid, rose, amber, moss, jade or teal. Fonts offers eight faces for the chat and four monospace faces for code and the terminal, all under the Open Font License, with one text size for all three.

title: Settings
text:
New sessions
Each agent’s mode, model and effort to start with. The pills under the composer change them for one session.

title: Settings
text:
Composer, Terminal, Files
Each has its own switches: which key sends and which languages are spell-checked; the terminal’s color scheme, its cursor, and whether a selection copies itself; format on save and its formatters.

title: Settings
text:
Updates and About
Updates checks daily, or when you ask, and installs the new version itself. About shows which version this is and who makes it.

title: Outline Panel
text:
Entries
Going back through a long session is a pain. The outline gives each prompt one entry, under a heading for each day: the time, then three to five words for what you asked. A short prompt is shown as it is. A long one is labeled by the agent’s small model, Haiku for Claude Code and Codex’s light model for Codex, in a separate session, so nothing enters yours. Labels are made for the entries in view, a few at a time, and kept, so each prompt is labeled once.

title: Outline Panel
text:
Going back
Click an entry and the chat glides back to that round. As you scroll, the entry in view is highlighted, so the outline always shows where you are. It shares the left side with the files: one shows at a time, and switching does not move the chat.

title: Get Started
text:
Open a project
Choose a folder, pick an agent, and type your first prompt. That starts a session in the folder, with a tab and a row in the sidebar. To pick up an older one, find it in the sidebar: every session on this computer is listed under its project, from both agents.
On the first launch, Emaki copies every Claude Code session into ~/.emaki/archive, and each later launch catches up, so a session Claude Code has deleted is still here. See Projects.

title: Get Started
text:
Layout
The sidebar and the chat are always there. The four panels are hidden by default: files or outline opens on the left of the chat, the shell or agent terminal on its right.





Projects


Chats


Files ⌘⇧F


Outline ⌘⇧O


Shell Terminal ⌘⇧S


Agent Terminal ⌘⇧A

title: Get Started
text:
What Emaki keeps
Everything Emaki keeps is in ~/.emaki:







archive/
every Claude Code session, copied byte for byte


logs/
each session rendered as markdown


search.db
the full-text index


config.json
your settings



Codex has its own archiving system, so archive/ only stores Claude Code sessions.
Emaki changes one setting in Claude Code: its status line, which feeds Emaki’s own status line under the composer. To put yours back, run emaki-core statusline restore.

title: Chats
text:
Transcript
Chat transcripts are well-rendered with high-quality interface. Agent tool calls are stacked to release reading pressure. You can expand them and even get summaries of each tool call to understand what happened. Artifacts, background jobs, subagents, Q&A sessions are all properly taken care of with smooth UI.

title: Chats
text:
Composer
Attach files by pasting, dropping, or the + button. @ picks a file or folder from the project, and / lists the agent’s slash commands and skills. Spelling and grammar are checked as you type.

We proudly recommend using Kotoba as your dictation app on Emaki or any other composer on your machine. It supports light-weighted models for voice-to-text dictation and post-processing.

title: Chats
text:
Mode, model and effort
By providing three pills under the composer, Emaki made it easy to toggle among different modes, models, and efforts without needing to trigger keyboard commands or / commands (though they are also supported).

title: Chats
text:
Status line
The row under the composer shows how much of the context window is used and where the 5-hour and 7-day limits stand. Its colors change according to the thresholds. The status line logic is from the Waza plugin by tw93.

title: About
text:
An emaki (絵巻) is a Japanese picture handscroll: a long painted scene held between two rolls, read by winding it from one to the other, a span at a time. It is a good name for a window whose job is an agent chat too long to see at once.
The app’s icon is a handscroll seen from the front, with an agent chat on its sheet: the agent on the left with its spark, your reply on the right. This one carries a landscape instead, and winds as you move across it.

title: About
text:
Why it exists
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays, thirty by default, with no warning. Every other tool in this space reads ~/.claude/projects and stops there, so they all inherit that expiry.
So Emaki copies first and renders second. The archive sweep runs before anything else touches a session, for exactly this reason: if rendering fails, the bytes are already safe. The archive is not a backup but a peer source: live and kept transcripts are read together, so a session Claude Code has deleted stays listed, searchable and readable, marked kept.
Compaction, for what it is worth, was never the threat: it appends a boundary and keeps writing to the same file, leaving the earlier rows intact.

title: About
text:
How it is built
Rust, with GPUI, the Zed editor’s UI framework, and gpui-component for the window. There is no daemon, no browser and no hook.
crates/emaki-core   everything without a window, and the CLI
crates/emaki-app    the window
vendor/             gpui-component, with a few changes of ours
scripts/            packaging, the icon, the status line
The core works in this order:

Adapters, one per agent, find each agent’s sessions on disk.
Archive copies Claude Code’s byte for byte, before anything else touches them.
Build parses the JSONL transcript into a model of rounds, items and tool calls. The transcript is the only source of truth.
Render writes that model as markdown under ~/.emaki/logs.
Search indexes every item in SQLite FTS5.

The app reads the same model and draws it. A file watcher says when to look again. To reply, it writes to a terminal session’s inbox, or runs a headless agent of its own that appends to the same transcript.

title: About
text:
Where it is going
Three stages. The first is a complete app for Claude Code: permanent history, organization by recency, project and agent, readable chats, and an explanation on any step. The second is the public release and the feedback that comes with it. The third extends the same to Codex, Kimi and the other mainstream coding agents, so Emaki works across all of them.
Codex arrived in v0.2.0, ahead of its stage; the releases are the honest record of where things stand.

title: About
text:
Who makes it



Alkaline Software
Two data scientists making basic software. Alkaline is the other word for basic, as a high pH is, and basic is what the software means to be: the things that should plainly exist. Emaki is one of them, a development environment for the agentic era that anyone who works with agents can use.



Dr John Paul Helveston
Associate Professor of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering at George Washington University.



Dr Pingfan Hu
Data scientist and developer at George Washington University, advised by John Paul.

title: About
text:
Credits
The home page’s figure follows the line-drawing manner of hairline’s figures: nothing filled, no words, what is far is dimmer, and one bright mark.
Icons are Tabler’s outline set, drawn at a stroke of 1.75 where Tabler’s own is 2, in the app and on this site. The file tree’s icons are Catppuccin’s. The code colors are Rosé Pine’s hues, retinted for contrast. The terminal keeps Kaku’s cream in the light appearance. Every face the app carries is under the SIL Open Font License, and so are this site’s: Source Serif 4, JetBrains Mono and Belleza. The site is made with Quarto.

title: Agent Terminal Panel
text:
The agent’s own screen
If you want your agent’s original CLI, this is the panel. Every session Emaki runs has a terminal behind it: Claude Code’s hidden one, or the one Codex’s driver joins. This panel shows it whole, at the chat’s right, so you can watch the agent work as in the CLI and type into it. It is the same terminal the chat reads from and types into, so answering here is the same as answering in the chat, and nothing is doubled. Pasted screenshots reach the agent as they would in the CLI.
Open it with nothing running and it starts the agent (Claude Code). Where it cannot start one, while a turn runs in a terminal of your own or in an archived session, it says why. Anything the agent asks that the chat has no card for can be answered here. It shares the right side with the shell terminal: one shows at a time.

title: Files Panel
text:
The tree
The project’s folder as a tree, with Catppuccin’s file icons and git’s marks: a letter on a changed file, a dot on a folder with changes inside, and ignored files dimmed. It works like a file manager: drag files in from Finder, drag rows to move them, cut, copy, duplicate, move to the Trash (⌘⌫) and undo (⌘Z). New File and New Folder are at the top, and a file the agent writes appears as soon as it lands.

title: Files Panel
text:
Open and edit
Click a file to open it in a pane between the tree and the chat; click it again to close it. The enlarge button gives the pane the chat’s room. ⌘S saves, ⌘W closes, and Emaki asks before anything unsaved is lost. Format on save covers ten languages and is off until you turn it on.
Code has line numbers, colors, and a gutter mark for each git change, with a card to see or revert it. Every kind of file is drawn for what it is:


Code every language, colored
Markdown as it reads, or as written
CSV and TSV a grid you can edit in place
Parquet a table with each column’s type
Word pages you can type in and format
Excel cells with their number formats
PowerPoint slides as they look
PDF sharp at any width, with search and page previews
HTML in the system’s web view
Pictures at their own size

title: Files Panel
text:
Git
In a repository, the branch’s name sits at the top of the tree. Click it to switch branches, make one (⌘⇧N) or publish one; Fetch and Pull are at the bottom of the list. If you switch with uncommitted changes, Emaki asks whether to leave them or bring them along, and switches only when every change can go where you asked.
The Changes pill (⌘⇧G) opens the Changes sheet: tick the files, write the message, commit (⌘↩︎) and push (⌘P). A changed picture shows before and after, side by side. History lists the commits: Undo takes back the newest while the remote does not have it, and Revert takes back any one as a new commit. Nothing is committed, pushed or pulled until you click to do it.

title: Projects
text:
Projects
All sessions in Emaki are project-based, all listed in the sidebar. You can pin your selected projects and show or hide sessions. To start a new session, you can either click the + button on an existing project or press ⌘T in the project you are in. With ⌘N, you can start one anywhere (the same as going to your landing page).

title: Projects
text:
Sessions

In the sidebar
Sessions are managed under their projects. A session’s leading logo tells you which agent it belongs to and lights up while the agent runs. A dot shows where the session stands, and a bar at the left marks one that is open in a tab. Claude Code and Codex sessions sit side by side, each read from the agent’s own files.


All Sessions
All Sessions (⌘L) lists every project and session with the day it was last used. This page provides plenty of ways of easily managing your existing sessions.

title: Projects
text:
Archiving
Claude Code deletes its transcripts after 30 days. Emaki copies each one into ~/.emaki/archive. Codex never deletes sessions by age, so Emaki reads them in place.
Archived sessions cannot be interacted. You can actively archive/unarchive your sessions. When you unarchive a Claude Code session, it will be treated as if it were created by the time you unarchive it.

title: Projects
text:
Tabs
Each open session is a tab, grouped by project. ⌘1 to ⌘9 switch tabs, ⌘W closes one, ⌘⇧T reopens the last one closed, and you can drag tabs to reorder them.

title: Shell Terminal Panel
section: A shell where the work is
text:
A shell where the work is
Opening a terminal and cd-ing to the project is easy, but doing it again and again is a pain. The shell terminal opens your login shell in the session’s folder, at the chat’s right. Shells are tabs: the + or ⌘T opens one, ⌘W closes it, ⌘K clears the screen, and you can drag tabs to reorder them. They stay open until you close them or quit.
Paste a picture and it lands as the path of a file. A selection can copy itself when you let go (Settings, Terminal). Programs that use the mouse get its clicks and scrolls, and the Mac’s line keys work (⌘←, ⌘→, ⌘⌫). The look is inspired by Kaku, in the window’s own colors and font.
The same shell opens beside the install steps on the Agents page, for the commands they give. It shares the right side with the agent terminal: one shows at a time.
